### ✨ Added

- **The components themselves, as source, in [`reference/react/`](https://github.com/junkerderprovinz/glimstone/tree/main/reference/react).** `Button`, `Toggle`, `Card`, `Badge`, `DropdownListbox`, `ConfirmDialog`, `Toast`, `InfoBubble`, `IconTipButton` and `AboutCard`, plus the four hooks they need. Until now this repository described what a control must look like and left the building of it to each app, which is where the family drifted: two apps built from the same document produced the same language in two dialects. One calls the switch `Toggle` in its own file, the other calls it `Switch` inside a shared `Field.tsx` beside six more controls; one has `ConfirmDialog`, the other `Confirm`; one has `DropdownListbox`, the other `Choice`; one keeps `Card` in a settings-page helper, the other in a `Shell.tsx`. Every one of those is a correct reading of the prose, and that is the problem: a rule written here then has to be applied by hand once per dialect, and a fix made in one app reads from the outside as the two apps simply disagreeing.
- **Three things the components deliberately do not carry, each for a reason that would otherwise force a fork.** No icon set, because which mark means "backup now" is the app's own vocabulary and not the language's: the assortment stays a specification in `glyphs.md` and an app registers its own resolver once, through `setGlyphResolver`, so a button can still pick its glyph by meaning rather than being handed one at every call site. No translation: every string is a prop. No data: the About card takes its version as a prop instead of reading a health endpoint, so one file serves apps whose endpoints differ.
- **The folder is self-contained and proven, not asserted.** Only two imports leave it, `../appearance.ts` and `../controls.ts`, and the whole set typechecks in strict mode against nothing but React, measured with `tsc --noEmit --strict` rather than claimed.

### 🎨 Design

- **The About card gets its order fixed, and the order is the standard.** It had a content list and no arrangement, which is why three adopting apps built three different cards from one section: one led with the sentence, one led with the versions, one put them in a two-column list of labelled fields. The order now: what this is, then the money with its own button, then the report with its own buttons, then the versions as a footer. The reason it matters is the pairing - each sentence sits directly above the thing it asks for. Three sentences stacked over one row of buttons reads as a form to work through; a sentence with its own button under it reads as one offer, and the card carries two.
- **One extra step of space above the report sentence, and only above that one.** At even spacing the coffee button sits as close to the sentence below it as to the one it belongs to, and the eye pairs it with the wrong text. A blank line is what separates two paragraphs everywhere else, and that is all this is.
- **A card never names a route no control on it can reach.** The sentence and the buttons under it are one promise. An app with no address of its own says "open an issue" and stops there, rather than inviting a mail that lands in another product's inbox: a contact route that reaches the wrong place is worse than no contact route, because somebody writes and then waits. Learned the other way round first, when a card offered a mail button pointing at a different product's address.
- **In the version footer, only the number is a link.** The word in front of it is not a destination, and underlining it as part of the link makes "Version" read as somewhere to go.
